text.text: KörkortGo
Swedish category B learning guide
A learning aid
2026 version
Before you begin

This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.

This book is for English-speaking learners preparing for ordinary Swedish category B driving. It connects rules with decisions you can explain and practise. It does not grant permission to drive, replace mandatory training or supervised practice, reproduce official examination questions, or guarantee a test result.
How to use this book

Begin with modules 1–3. They establish personal readiness, vehicle preparation and road interpretation. Use modules 4–7 to apply that foundation in traffic and changing conditions. Modules 8–9 develop responsibility for the vehicle, its load and the journey's impact. Module 10 brings the learning together.

Each lesson contains a goal, an explanation, an original worked situation, a knowledge check with its answer, and a short reminder. After each module, write a reflection and use it to plan your next study or supervised practice session. Explain the answer before reading it; then change one condition in the example and consider whether your decision would change.
Read, reflect and practise
Read the labels

children.text: Learning approaches, worked decisions and review guides

text.text: are original teaching material. They help you apply the principles; they are not additional laws. English explanations are written for learning and do not replace the Swedish legal wording.
Use the official references

References appear beside factual material. Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen provide the main guidance. Official legislation and other public authorities supply details missing from the main agency guidance. Selected manufacturer handbooks supply missing technical cautions and are listed separately. The lessons identify source limits and distinguish recommendations, research and teaching inferences from legal duties. Use the handbook for the actual vehicle; a generic example is not its operating procedure.
Check current guidance

Original licensing, examination and vehicle checks are dated 1 October 2026; added passages have their own checks on 12–13 October. Check current official information before using a time-sensitive rule. Hypothetical numbers in examples are identified as such and are not measurements of your vehicle or personal performance.
Your learning journey

label.text: Prepare a car that is ready
Take responsibility for the vehicle and load
Reduce the impact of each journey

Sources and references

Driving begins with a choice: whether this person, this vehicle and this journey are ready to go together. Sweden’s Vision Zero (Nollvisionen) aims for no one to be killed or seriously injured in traffic. The choices taught here contribute to that aim.
Learning rules matters, but so does recognising when a different plan is safer. This module helps you build both habits.
In this chapter

label.text: M01-L03 · Pressure is a driving risk
M01-L04 · Plan the journey before the ignition

text.text: This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.
Original sources checked 4 October 2026; G1 additions checked 12 October 2026. Consult current official guidance and applicable rules.
No. The amendment has transitional rules for tests taken before 19 August. Confirm the applicable expiry in the official result information.
Build a personal preparation checklist covering entitlement, permits, supervised practice, risk training and examinations.

For an ordinary new category B licence, you need a valid learner permit, permanent residence in Sweden or at least six months of study here, the minimum age of 18, valid car risk training, and successful theory and practical tests. Holding another EEA licence affects the application route. Category B normally covers a passenger car or light goods vehicle with a registered maximum weight of no more than 3,500 kg; trailers are explained in module 8. Check any conditions on your entitlement, including an automatic-transmission restriction.

Private practice requires an approved supervisor for the particular learner. The learner normally needs a group 1 permit. Practice in a passenger car can begin at 16; the minimum is 17 years and 6 months for practice with a light goods vehicle or a light trailer. The supervisor is legally treated as the driver, must carry proof of approval, and the practice sign must be clearly visible from behind. Exceptions concerning an existing entitlement must be checked against your own circumstances.

The introductory-course requirement for private practice ended on 1 August 2026. Supervisor approval still applies. This change does not remove mandatory risk training. A theory test passed on or after 19 August 2026 is valid for one year. Tests passed before that date retain the earlier rules; Trafikverket describes the ordinary earlier validity as four months. Check your own result and any approved extension rather than adding a year yourself.
Apply the learning

Risk training has two parts: the first covers alcohol, drugs, fatigue and other risky behaviour; the second covers speed, safety and differing road/weather conditions, including slippery-road training. It must be completed before the tests and remains valid until the licence is obtained or for at most five years. Car and motorcycle risk training are not interchangeable.

Record your permit, supervisor approval if practising privately, entitlement conditions, risk-training status, test preparation and any support application. Use actual expiry dates from your records. Schedule practice around skills you need to improve, not only around an available test slot.

Noor plans to practise privately in September 2026. Her relative says no approvals are needed because a course was abolished. Noor checks the current supervisor page and waits for supervisor approval. The removed course and the retained approval are different requirements.
Does a theory pass from July 2026 automatically become valid for a year?
Plan the administrative route and the learning route together.

objectives.text: Build a personal preparation checklist covering entitlement, permits, supervised practice, risk training and examinations.

text.text: (1) No. The driver must still be capable of driving safely. The prescription exception to the narcotics rule does not excuse unsafe impairment. (2) Microsleep is a brief unintended sleep episode, not a deliberate action. (3) No. Adequate sleep addresses sleep deprivation; stimulation can mask fatigue and produce overconfidence without safe judgement.
Decide whether to drive when tiredness, illness, medication, alcohol or drugs may affect you, and explain a safer alternative.
You must not drive when illness, exhaustion, alcohol, other substances or another condition prevents safe control. A legal alcohol threshold is not a guarantee that you are capable of driving safely.

Trafikverket states that the blood-alcohol limit for drink-driving is 0.2 per mille. For an aggravated offence, factors include at least 1.0 per mille, substantial impairment, or driving that creates a clear traffic danger. Non-prescribed narcotics are subject to a zero-tolerance rule. Properly prescribed medication does not make impaired driving acceptable.

Alcohol can affect judgement, attention, vision, reactions and coordination. Feeling normal does not measure those effects. Performance can remain impaired the next day. Do not use a fixed number of hours, a shower, coffee or a calculation as a personal clearance to drive. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about medicines and driving; do not change a prescribed treatment simply to make a journey.

label.text: Trafikverket: effects of alcohol and medicines

text.text: Before taking the keys, ask: Can I stay alert? Can I see and move well enough? Has anything changed since I last drove? Can I concentrate on several developing situations? If the answers are uncertain, make a different travel plan and resolve the uncertainty first. Medical eligibility and day-to-day readiness are related but different: having a licence does not mean you are fit for every journey.
Sleep and safe judgement

Microsleep (mikrosömn) is a brief, unintended episode of sleep. You do not choose it or reliably prevent it by deciding to try harder. For a deliberately hypothetical two-second lapse at a constant 90 km/h, distance = speed × time: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 metres per second; 25 × 2 = 50 metres travelled while asleep. Two seconds is an example, not a prediction of how long a microsleep lasts.

children.text: Official safety advice · Replace missing sleep with sleep.

text.text: Adequate sleep is the fundamental remedy for sleep deprivation. Coffee or an energy drink may briefly make you feel more alert, but does not replace the sleep you need; serious sleep deprivation can still lead to microsleep. Music, an open window or willpower should not be treated as a clearance to drive: they do not provide the missing sleep. Do not start when you cannot stay awake; if sleepiness develops, stop somewhere safe and arrange rest or another way to travel. See
for planning around fatigue on a journey.

children.text: Medical explanation · Stimulation is not safe judgement.

text.text: Stimulant misuse, for example involving amphetamine or cocaine, can produce overconfidence while judgement and concentration are impaired. Some stimulant effects can reduce the feeling of fatigue or drowsiness: tiredness may be masked rather than the need for sleep removed. Feeling energetic is therefore not proof of safe driving ability. Effects vary with substance, dose and individual circumstances; this does not mean every prescribed stimulant treatment has the same effect. Ask your prescriber about your treatment and driving.

label.text: Swedish Government: stimulant confidence and judgement

text.text: Lina slept too little before an evening journey. She suggests an energy drink and loud music; her friend suggests a stimulant to make her feel confident. The missing sleep remains unresolved, and a stronger feeling of alertness cannot certify safe judgement. She postpones the drive or arranges an alert driver, and makes time for adequate sleep before driving again.
Apply the learning

caption.text: A tired learner and a companion pause beside a parked car. The keys remain on the bench.

text.text: A driver has taken a new medicine and feels unusually drowsy. A passenger offers to keep talking to help them stay awake. The safer choice is to arrange another driver or transport and ask for medication advice. Conversation does not resolve the impairment.

(1) Is driving automatically acceptable if a medicine was prescribed correctly? (2) How does microsleep differ from choosing to close your eyes? (3) A sleep-deprived driver feels energetic and unusually confident after taking a stimulant. Has the missing sleep been remedied, and does that feeling establish safe judgement?
Decide fitness before deciding convenience.

objectives.text: Decide whether to drive when tiredness, illness, medication, alcohol or drugs may affect you, and explain a safer alternative.

text.text: (1) Observed performance. Confidence is useful only when it agrees with what you can actually do. (2) Its central aim is that no one should be killed or seriously injured in traffic. Safer driver choices contribute to that aim.
Identify how peers, impulses, confidence and personal circumstances can change a decision, and rehearse a refusal or alternative.

The official education syllabus asks learners to reflect on social influence, impulsive decisions, personal motives and their own limitations. These are skills to practise, not labels to attach to an age group or personality.

Separate the journey's purpose from the feeling of the moment. “Get everyone home” is a purpose. “Show that I can handle this bend quickly” is a different motive. When a passenger's request changes your speed, following distance or willingness to overtake, name the change before acting on it.

A useful personal boundary is a sentence you can use without debate: “I will stop somewhere safe before changing the route”; “I am not passing here”; or “We need another way home.” These are original rehearsal tools, not official scripts. Practise them before a difficult situation, and agree that passengers will help with navigation only when asked.
You still owe care to other road users and must adapt speed to conditions. Cooperation does not authorise ignoring a traffic rule because another person is impatient.

Nollvisionen means no one should be killed or seriously injured in traffic. It is not a promise that nobody will ever make a mistake. Trafikverket describes shared responsibility: road users must show consideration and judgement and follow traffic rules, while system designers have ultimate responsibility for the system’s safety. Your part includes choosing safe speed and margins and refusing a pressured manoeuvre; road and vehicle design also contribute. For example, staying behind a vehicle near a hidden crest helps protect people even when a passenger dislikes the delay.
Apply the learning

caption.text: A passenger talks to the driver. In the road view, the car remains behind a van near a crest. Illustration, not a scale diagram of following distance.

text.text: Friends laugh when Amir stays behind a slow vehicle on a road with a hidden crest. He recognises the urge to prove himself, maintains space and waits for a genuinely suitable opportunity. His decision protects the purpose of the trip: arriving safely. There is no need to “win” the interaction.

(1) Which is better evidence of readiness: feeling confident, or repeatedly identifying hazards and responding safely during supervised practice? (2) Does Vision Zero aim only to reduce minor collisions, or to prevent deaths and serious injuries?
A decision can be socially uncomfortable and still be the correct driving decision.

objectives.text: Identify how peers, impulses, confidence and personal circumstances can change a decision, and rehearse a refusal or alternative.

text.text: The arrival expectation. Inform the people waiting, choose a different mode or postpone if necessary. A late start does not change the rules or stopping space needed.
Compare route, departure time, travel mode and passenger choices for safety, accessibility and environmental impact.
Official advice · Trafikverket

Trafikverket recommends checking forecasts and traffic conditions, allowing time, taking breaks on longer trips and preparing supplies appropriate to the season. The education syllabus also asks you to consider whether a car is the right means of transport and how passengers or timing affect a journey.

Plan a usable journey rather than an ideal arrival time. Check where you can rest, refuel or charge as appropriate to the vehicle, and stop legally at the destination. Arrange restraints and space for passengers before departure. If the route has unfamiliar junctions or restrictions, identify them while parked.

Compare realistic alternatives. Walking, cycling or public transport may suit some journeys; a car may be necessary for others. Consider access needs, luggage, the return trip and the conditions at the time you will actually travel. A plan that depends on rushing after a late appointment is already fragile.
Apply the learning

caption.text: Viewed over their shoulders, two people study a digital map on a tablet facing them. Rain falls outside. The map is illustrative, not live route guidance.

text.text: A learner and supervisor can practise on a familiar route in daylight or travel through an unfamiliar town during a forecast snow shower. They choose daylight practice today and plan a later lesson for more demanding conditions with suitable preparation. text.text: (1) No; establish operation while stationary. (2) A remaining circuit can retain some braking after one fails, with reduced capability. (3) Keep firm continuous pressure and steer as needed; normal ABS pulsation is not a reason to pump. (4) Sinking can suggest a hydraulic leak or fault; sponginess can suggest air. Obtain professional assessment before an unsafe journey. (5) Excessive current; the fuse interrupts the circuit.
Explain the purpose of core controls, warning indicators, braking and steering systems, and identify when further instructions are needed.

The practical test can include checking steering, brakes, tyres, lighting, fluids and warning systems. You should be able to explain why you check them and propose action if you find a problem. Before moving, adjust the seat, head restraint, steering wheel, mirrors and belt.

While parked, locate the service brake, parking brake, transmission controls, indicators, lighting controls, wipers, washers, demisting and hazard lights. Explain what each control is for, then demonstrate it with your supervisor. “I can find it” and “I can use it without losing attention” are different learning stages.

The service brake is used to reduce speed and stop; the parking brake helps secure a stationary vehicle. Steering changes the vehicle's direction, but the tyres and road must provide the forces needed to follow that direction. Braking and steering share the available friction: turning the wheel is not proof that the car can follow the intended path.

Control layouts, warning meanings and system checks differ. Use the instructions for the actual vehicle before trying an unfamiliar function. This material does not prescribe a universal brake-servo test, fluid-opening procedure or response to every dashboard symbol. An unexplained warning is a reason to establish what is wrong before treating the car as ready.
Brakes and protective circuits

children.text: Technical explanation · Brakes and electrical protection.

text.text: Separate brake circuits provide a reserve: if one circuit fails, the remaining circuit can still provide some braking. This reduces the chance of losing all braking through one circuit fault. Remaining braking may be weaker; it is not permission to continue normally. The technical requirements distinguish the surviving capability from full service-brake performance.

Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering control. During an emergency stop with ABS, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer as necessary; do not pump the pedal. Pulsation or vibration through the pedal during ABS operation can be normal feedback as the system regulates braking. This differs from a changed pedal feel in ordinary braking. ABS does not guarantee a shorter stop or create grip that the tyres lack.

The table gives possibilities, not diagnoses. A sinking pedal can suggest internal leakage, although some servo/pump behaviour can resemble it. Air can cause hydraulic pedal sponginess. Obtain professional assessment for an unexplained change.

Organise a safety check of tyres, lights, visibility and vehicle condition, and distinguish a defect from a reason to seek help.

Work around the car, then through the driving position. Look for damaged tyres, an unusual stance, leaks or obstructions; confirm that windows and mirrors permit a useful view. Check required lights and indicators, and ask for help where a second person is useful. Check washers and wipers before you need them in poor weather. Use the actual vehicle's instructions for fluid levels and service checks. These groups reflect the official practical-test safety check; they are not a guarantee that a quick walkaround detects every defect.

Tyres must be suitable for the vehicle, including load capacity and applicable speed capability. The registration information and approved vehicle requirements matter when changing tyre sizes. Do not assume any wheel that physically fits is suitable.

Required lighting must work and be used appropriately. Some cars can run daytime lights without rear lights; the driver must ensure suitable front, rear and side lighting is on in darkness, twilight or poor weather. A trailer's lighting must be on during travel. Automatic settings may need manual intervention.

Uneven mass distribution around a rotating wheel and tyre can cause steering vibration, sometimes most noticeable at particular speeds. Wheel imbalance is one possible cause, not a diagnosis: tyre damage and other wheel or steering defects may also be involved. Arrange assessment rather than testing the symptom by driving faster.

text.text: (1) No. Trip length does not make it safe. (2) It helps limit damaging head movement and reduce neck-injury risk, particularly in rear impacts. (3) The seat supports the relatively heavy head and body together and takes collision forces, protecting the vulnerable neck. (4) Controlled deformation absorbs energy and slows the compartment more gradually, reducing occupant forces.
Select suitable restraints for passengers and explain how belts, headrests and airbags work together.

In an ordinary car journey, occupants must use an available belt-equipped place and wear the belt. Children under 135 cm normally need an appropriate child restraint. The driver must take appropriate measures to ensure passengers under 15 use the required protection. Limited exceptions exist, including specified short occasional journeys, and should not become a routine travel plan.

For a child aged three or more but shorter than 135 cm, an occasional short transport without an available child restraint is an exception only under the stated conditions: use the belt where possible and not the front seat of a passenger car or light goods vehicle. For a child under three, the exception is an occasional short taxi trip, also excluding the front seat. Plan with the correct restraint instead.

Trafikverket recommends rear-facing travel until at least four to five years, preferably longer. Transportstyrelsen's advice says as long as possible, normally around four. These are recommendations, not a single legal birthday on which to turn the seat. Choose equipment that fits the child and car and stays within its approved size and weight limits. Reaching 135 cm does not automatically produce good adult-belt fit.

Never place a rear-facing child restraint in front of an active passenger airbag. Trafikverket advises at least 140 cm in front of an active airbag unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise; Transportstyrelsen gives more conservative advice for children in restraints. Resolve seating and airbag compatibility using the vehicle and restraint instructions before travelling. An airbag supplements a belt; it does not replace one. Adjust the head restraint for the person occupying the seat.
How protection works

In a rear impact, the seat and torso can move while the head lags behind. A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided.

A young child's head is relatively heavy and the neck is vulnerable. In a frontal collision, a rear-facing seat supports the head and body together, takes up collision forces and distributes the load across the supported body. The neck does not have to restrain the heavy head on its own in the same way as when facing forwards. This is why the recommendations above concern protection, not only seat orientation. Follow the seat's size limits, fitting instructions and airbag compatibility.

label.text: Trafikverket: child head and neck protection

text.text: Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the occupants' space. Spreading the deceleration over a longer time reduces forces acting on the people inside. A car remaining visually undamaged is not the objective: designed deformation can be part of its protection. Belts and suitable child restraints still matter, and no structure makes every collision survivable.

Plan observation and control for starting, stopping, reversing, hill starts and turning, and explain why supervised practice is needed.

Before moving away from the edge, changing position or lane, you must ensure the movement can be made without danger or unnecessary obstruction. Turning around and reversing must be possible without danger or obstruction to other road users. Signal your intention where required, but a signal does not give you priority.

Break a manoeuvre into preparation, observation, controlled movement and reassessment. Choose a place with enough room; check around the vehicle and along the intended path; move only while the space remains safe. Stop and reassess when the view changes. Looking once before starting is not continuous observation.

A hill start is a control task: prevent unintended movement while coordinating the actual vehicle's transmission, brakes and accelerator. Do not copy pedal sequences between cars without instruction. Reversing, parking and turning also need practical feedback about vehicle dimensions and the path followed by its corners. The official practical test may examine these skills, including effective braking. Practise braking exercises only in suitable, supervised conditions—not as an experiment in ordinary traffic.

Interpret signs, panels, markings and signals together, including authorised directions.

Follow the traffic instructions that apply to you. Where an instruction differs from a general traffic rule, the instruction governs. A steady traffic-light indication takes precedence over a yield or stop sign; a police officer's direction takes precedence over the rules and ordinary traffic instructions. This is not a rule that a green signal cancels every other restriction. Authorised guards also give traffic directions that must be followed.

For ordinary vehicle signals: red means stop; red and amber together still mean stop, with green approaching. Green permits movement, subject to other duties and space ahead. Amber means stop unless, when green changes to amber, you are already so close that stopping would be dangerous. Flashing amber requires particular caution; read the signs and applicable rules. Arrow signals apply to the direction indicated.

Ordinary vehicle signals Red, red/amber, green and amber appear in that order. Flashing amber is a separate condition, not the next stage of the normal cycle. Arrow indications apply to the direction shown.

Explain how observation, speed, reaction, braking, grip and following space affect your options.

Choose a speed that preserves control and lets you stop within the road you can see and before a foreseeable obstruction. Your distance from the vehicle ahead must allow for it slowing or stopping. Weather, visibility, road condition, vehicle condition and loading all matter.

For an ordinary car, the general speed limits are 50 km/h within a built-up area and 70 km/h outside it, unless another applicable limit has been prescribed. The motorway default is 110 km/h; 120 km/h can be prescribed. Local and road-specific limits often differ, and a lower vehicle-combination limit still applies. Read the current signs and conditions rather than selecting a speed from the road’s appearance.

Think of stopping in two parts. During the time between noticing a hazard and beginning effective braking, the vehicle still travels. After that, it travels while slowing. More speed consumes more distance during the same delay and increases the energy that must be removed. Less available friction reduces what the tyres can do for braking and steering.
Continue the learning

children.text: Illustrative calculation, not a stopping-distance prediction.

text.text: A speed of 50 km/h is approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second, that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added.

Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every condition.

children.text: Safety advice · Check a timed gap.

text.text: For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing the road while counting.

The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on “two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents 60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without requiring you to estimate metres by eye.
Margins and braking distance

children.text: Safety advice · When someone follows too closely.

text.text: Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean withholding it.

Maya has a close follower and sees brake lights farther ahead. She eases off early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she can reduce the need for a sudden stop.
With the same effective grip and braking deceleration on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared:

. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 × deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated assumptions.

Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about 12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the total does
quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are not predicted stopping distances for your car.
A rough calculation method

children.text: Approximate exercise model · Keep the methods separate.

text.text: Define v as speed in km/h and t as the supplied reaction time in seconds. Exact constant-speed reaction distance is (v ÷ 3.6) × t metres; braking is not included. When an exercise specifies the rough method below, use both rough estimates together rather than substituting an exact reaction value.
R = (v ÷ 10) × t × 3 metres. Divide speed by ten, multiply by the supplied seconds, then by three.

documents the one-second shortcut; multiplication by a supplied t is editorial proportional arithmetic. Half a second gives half the one-second estimate; two seconds gives twice it. These are supplied exercise inputs, not claims about every driver's reaction time.
B = (v ÷ 10)² × 0.4 metres. Divide speed by ten, square that result, then multiply by 0.4.

describes this shortcut under good-brake, good-tyre and dry-asphalt assumptions. The coefficient is an exercise assumption, not a universal result for a real car or road. Supplied reaction time does not change the braking part in this model.

S = R + B. Calculate both parts separately with metres, then add. Keep decimal precision during the working; round only the final result if a precision is requested. These shortcuts teach arithmetic, not a safe-distance guarantee or a prediction for an actual hazard.
Trafiko is a commercial teaching source, cited only for these approximate shortcuts.

supports reaction plus braking and dependence on speed and conditions, but does not supply these constants. Its illustrated distances have different assumptions and must not be mixed with this model. Real stopping depends on grip, gradient, tyres, brakes, response and other conditions. Retain the exact conversion and separate constant-deceleration comparison above under their own assumptions.

Where two vehicle paths cross, the general rule is to yield to a vehicle approaching from your right, except where another applicable rule or instruction determines the relationship. text.text: When stopped waiting to turn left across oncoming traffic, keep your front wheels pointing straight ahead. Your indicator communicates the intended turn; your wheels do not need to point along that intended route while you wait. If a vehicle hits you from behind, front wheels already turned left can direct the pushed car into oncoming traffic. Keeping them straight helps reduce that risk, but cannot guarantee protection in a collision. Begin steering into the turn only when there is a safe opportunity to make it.

Show particular consideration for children, older people, school patrols and people whose disability or illness is apparent and affects their use of traffic. Reduce speed appropriately near children, stopped passenger transport and other situations with foreseeable risks. Give pedestrians sufficient room and time when meeting or passing them.

text.text: Look for the space a person needs, not only the space they occupy now. A child may be hidden by a parked car. A cyclist may need to move out from an obstruction. A wheelchair user may need a usable kerb transition. You cannot reliably infer someone's hearing, vision or intentions from a quick glance. Allow time and observe their movement rather than demanding a response through the horn.
Observe people and possible movement Children, cyclists and riders have different needs. Sensory-impairment panels are separate examples; absence of a sign does not prove absence of risk.

Horses and riders also belong in your traffic assessment. Vehicle rules apply to riding and leading horses in relevant respects; they are not simply pedestrians because they travel slowly. Give them an unhurried, spacious interaction, and avoid unnecessary noise. This is a cautious application of the general duty of care, not a fixed passing-distance rule.
Horses and riders This warning supports early observation. It does not specify a fixed passing distance.

Where the maximum permitted speed is 50 km/h or lower, a driver approaching a bus whose driver signals to leave a bus stop must slow and give it the opportunity to leave, stopping if needed. The bus driver must also take particular care. If passing on the right of a bus or tram stopped at a stop without a refuge, stop to allow boarding or alighting passengers free passage.
Recognise a bus stop and speed limit The bus-stop marker and the 40 km/h speed sign are independent examples. The bus marker itself does not set the speed limit.

A bus indicator does not create unconditional priority, and the higher road limit does not excuse deliberately blocking it.

text.text: Do not pet, call to or talk to a working guide dog to attract its attention. Distraction can endanger the person it is helping. Allow the pair room and time; if you need to communicate, address the handler rather than trying to direct the dog. The handler chooses the route and remains in control. For example, a passenger beside your parked car wants to greet a guide dog at a crossing. Ask them to leave it working and keep the path clear.

Identify risks from bends, crests, narrow roads, animals and slow vehicles and justify speed and position changes.

Keep right when meeting another vehicle and leave a safe lateral gap. If an obstruction on your side prevents a safe meeting, stop if necessary to let the approaching vehicle pass. Your speed must suit the visible road and foreseeable hazards, with particular care at bends, crests and narrow meetings.

Read the road in sections: the visible straight, the entry to a bend, the portion hidden behind a crest and the next place someone might join. Never extend the clear section in your imagination. A vehicle emerging from a field or a cyclist beyond a bend changes what seemed to be an empty road.

Recognise animal warnings Each animal symbol has its own meaning. These examples do not imply that unpictured animals are absent.

Continue the learning

A slow vehicle's appearance may resemble a car even when its permitted speed and construction differ. Trafikverket advises other drivers to keep distance and pass only where appropriate. Stay far enough back to see around it and evaluate the road, rather than moving close to demand that it hurry.
Slow vehicles and following space The 50 m shown on
is a particular signed minimum distance, not a universal following gap for slow vehicles.

children.text: Turn planning · Choose a safer approach.

text.text: On an ordinary two-way rural road, heavy traffic may make a direct left turn unsafe. Continue to a suitable, permitted place or route where you can change direction safely, then return to approach the destination with a right turn if that movement is allowed and safe. This can avoid hazardous waiting and crossing the opposing stream at the original entrance. It is a planning alternative, not permission to turn around immediately on the carriageway. If no safe legal return route exists, choose another route or postpone.

label.text: Trafikverket: example of routing to a turning place

text.text: Before turning or leaving the road, protect oncoming traffic and traffic on the road you enter; take particular care of following traffic. A turnaround must cause neither danger nor obstruction. Signs and access restrictions still apply. Never turn around or reverse on a motorway or expressway. If you can wait safely and legally for a left turn, remember the advice in
to keep the front wheels straight; that advice does not make an unsafe turn suitable.

A farm entrance is on your left and busy traffic leaves no safe opportunity. You continue to an accessible junction route that legally and safely brings you back in the opposite direction. The entrance is then on your right. Check people, traffic and the entrance again before turning; the revised route does not guarantee a safe final movement.

Give extra attention at dawn and dusk, near animal habitats and where fences end or have openings. Scan woodland edges, bushes and small waterways beside the road: Trafikverket's road-project study describes these as animal routes that can conceal an approach. Its national guidance also describes animal passages through fence openings. These are cues for observation and speed planning, not predictions that animals only cross there.

At dusk, woodland meets a field beside a gap in the fence. Read the edges and opening as possible animal approaches, and choose speed for the view and foreseeable hazard. Keep observing even on fenced stretches. Prevention belongs here; actions after a wildlife collision are in
Make room at the narrowing

caption.text: Narrow bridge: the obstruction is on the teal driver’s right and the van approaches in its own lane. Reduce speed before the narrowing and stop if necessary. The scene does not measure a safe lateral gap.

text.text: You approach a narrow bridge with a van coming towards you and an obstruction on your side. You reduce speed before the narrowing and stop if necessary. Do not move into the van's path simply because you reached the obstruction first.
Check your understanding

(1) No vehicle is visible beyond a crest. Is the road proved clear? (2) Heavy traffic makes your rural left turn unsafe. What alternative can you plan? (3) Which time and roadside cues call for extra wildlife attention?
Let what you can actually see determine the available space.

objectives.text: Identify risks from bends, crests, narrow roads, animals and slow vehicles and justify speed and position changes.

text.text: No. Reassess and take the safest available action; do not treat finishing as more important than avoiding a collision. Plan with enough margin that abandoning is possible before committing.
Compare waiting with overtaking using visibility, speed difference, space and a safe completion path.

Overtake only without danger and with sufficient clear road. Do not start when a following driver has begun overtaking, or pass on the left when the vehicle ahead signals an intended leftward movement. Leave safe lateral clearance and a safe return opportunity. When being overtaken, do not increase speed or otherwise make the pass harder.

The normal passing side is left. Exceptions include a vehicle turning or clearly preparing to turn left, and the specified rules for marked same-direction lanes on roads limited to 70 km/h or less. Passing in queues or destination lanes has separate provisions; it does not remove the need to protect people at crossings.

Overtaking is generally prohibited immediately before or in a road junction, with specified exceptions for right-side overtaking, police/signal control, or an established yielding/stopping duty on the crossing road. Similar restrictions apply at level crossings, with exceptions for barriers or road-junction-type traffic signals. At an obscured bend or crest, do not use an opposing lane to overtake; the detailed provision contains limited exceptions. Section 39 also contains an exception for passing two-wheeled vehicles without sidecars. That exception does not override the danger prohibition, continuous-line restrictions or the uncontrolled-crossing prohibition. None of these exceptions proves a manoeuvre safe.

Do not overtake immediately before or on an uncontrolled pedestrian crossing, uncontrolled cycle passage or cycle crossing. Where parallel-lane passing is legally not classified as overtaking, the special crossing rule still requires a speed allowing an immediate stop for a person on the crossing or passage. Obey signs and continuous-line restrictions as well.
Overtaking signs and line information The prohibition and its end form a pair. For combined lines, identify the line nearest your lane.
warns of a coming centre-line or divider change; it is not an ordinary lane-change arrow.
Line information

Assess the whole passing path

Before moving, identify the full pass and return path, not merely the first gap. If completing it depends on another driver braking or on exceeding the limit, decline it. Small apparent time savings are not a reason to consume every margin.

caption.text: Following a slower vehicle towards a hidden bend. The visible straight does not establish a complete pass and return path. The depicted spacing is illustrative, not a recommended following distance.

text.text: A vehicle ahead travels slightly slower than you want. An approaching bend hides the final part of the pass. You stay behind at a useful distance. The first few clear metres do not establish a complete overtaking opportunity.
Check your understanding
If the vehicle ahead accelerates during your pass, must you complete it at any cost?
Choosing not to pass is a complete decision.

objectives.text: Compare waiting with overtaking using visibility, speed difference, space and a safe completion path.

text.text: (1) No. Use the lower applicable road/vehicle limit and reduce further for conditions. (2) Perception may have adapted to the motorway pace. Check the speedometer and current limit, then adapt to visibility and hazards. Feeling slow alone does not prove a faulty instrument or justify accelerating.
Plan motorway entry, lane choice, separation and exit, including a missed exit.

Motorways are for eligible motor vehicles and combinations designed and permitted to travel at least 40 km/h; class I mopeds are excluded. This is an eligibility condition, not a command to maintain 40 km/h in a queue. Enter and leave through the designated starts, ends and access routes. Do not reverse, turn around, use the central divider or cross-connections, or stop outside designated parking/rest areas except as an unavoidable incident requires. The relevant restrictions also apply to expressways (
) and their access routes.
Motorways and expressways Matched start/end pairs. The road regime does not override vehicle eligibility or the need to reduce speed for conditions. Motorway
Continue the learning
Expressway
Continue the learning

In an acceleration lane, adapt speed to the traffic in the lane you intend to join and enter as soon as it can be done without danger or unnecessary obstruction. A safe joining movement is your responsibility; other drivers who notice the intended entry must adapt speed to facilitate it. Entry without an acceleration lane has a yielding rule.

Read the joining-road layout Independent joining and lane-configuration examples. A road retaining its own lane differs from an acceleration lane; visual resemblance alone does not establish priority.
Continue the learning

Normally use the rightmost lane intended for your vehicle. Keep a following distance suited to speed, visibility and conditions; do not copy a car ahead that is following too closely. Signs may establish a lower maximum than a road's general limit, and your vehicle combination may have a lower limit again.

label.text: Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 7, chapter 4 §20 and chapter 9 §1

text.text: For an exit, take the suitable lane in good time and enter the deceleration lane as soon as possible. If you miss the exit, continue to a permitted exit and re-plan; never reverse to recover it. A breakdown is dealt with in
, not by using the shoulder as a convenient place to check navigation.
Prepare the exit early Independent navigation examples, not a single continuous route connecting the printed destinations. The separation marker does not authorise a late lane change.

Adjust after faster traffic

children.text: After the motorway · Recheck your speed.

text.text: After a long period at a steady motorway speed, your perception can adapt to that pace. On a slower road, the correct lower speed may feel unusually slow. This effect is often called speed adaptation or velocitation. Check the speedometer regularly to judge actual speed and adjust to the current limit and conditions. The feeling alone is not evidence that the speedometer is faulty.

label.text: ODOT: speed perception and speedometer checks

text.text: After a long motorway trip, you leave onto a road signed 50 km/h. At 50, the car feels as if it is crawling. Confirm the speedometer reading, read the new road and retain a speed suited to its limit, visibility and hazards. Do not accelerate merely to recover the motorway's familiar feeling.
Plan entry and exit

caption.text: Acceleration-lane detail: the teal car approaches traffic already on the main carriageway. Judge speed and a safe joining opportunity; this still image does not guarantee a usable gap.
Exit detail: plan the receiving lane early. If the necessary move cannot be made safely, continue to a permitted exit and re-plan; never reverse to recover the route.

text.text: Your exit sign appears while another vehicle occupies the lane you would need to cross. You do not force the move. You continue safely and tell your passenger the route will change.
Check your understanding

(1) Does a posted motorway limit override a lower trailer-combination limit? (2) After prolonged motorway driving, the lower speed on your new road feels too slow. What explains that feeling, and what should guide your speed?
Prepare the next movement before the road makes it urgent.

text.text: Evacuate people, get away from the railway and call 112. A disabled vehicle and a vehicle still able to drive through a barrier require different responses.
Interpret railway-crossing and roadworks information and approach changed lanes, queues and barriers safely.

Approach with particular care and at a speed that allows a stop before the crossing. Do not enter when a train or tram is approaching, a red signal shows, an audible warning sounds, a barrier is lowering, lowered or rising, or you might have to stop on the tracks. Cross without unnecessary delay only when it is permitted and there is room beyond.

Railway warnings and crossing controls Advance warnings, three/two/one countdown markers, crossbucks and active controls have different roles. Countdown boards do not specify fixed metre intervals. A still image does not reproduce flashing or sound. No crossing-ID number is invented. Advance warnings

Trafikverket says that if warnings begin while you are already crossing, continue out. If a functioning vehicle is trapped between the barriers, drive through the barrier to leave the tracks. If the vehicle has broken down on the tracks, evacuate everyone promptly, move well away and call 112. Give the crossing ID from the crossbuck sign if available without returning to danger. Do not stay on the tracks attempting a repair or pushing exercise.

Expect changed lanes, reduced speeds, workers and queues. Follow the current signs, signals and authorised guard directions; allow room around work areas and keep distance. A familiar road may now have a different usable path. Temporary guidance deserves attention before you reach the first barrier, not after you have entered the work area.

Roadworks and temporary guidance Independent recognition sets, not one verified work-zone layout. Keep directional, diagonal and horizontal markers distinct. Actual signs, signals and authorised directions govern the route. Warnings

-R · Review and self-assessment Answers and review guidance Official references This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.

(1) No; reassess safe speed for the view. (2) No. Front fog lights may replace dipped beam in fog/heavy precipitation. (3) Central vision reads fine detail; peripheral vision can detect movement/hazards. Look directly to inspect. (4) No. It may be a wider car with a failed lamp; preserve clearance.
Choose a visibility and lighting strategy for darkness, fog and glare.

Your speed must allow a stop within the visible road and before foreseeable hazards. Darkness does not create a separate allowance to travel beyond the distance you can assess. Keep the required lamps on; daytime running lights alone may be insufficient when conditions deteriorate.
Another changing condition: crosswinds Independent crosswind warnings. The windsock shows the wind direction; neither example is a fog warning or a headlight instruction.
Continue the learning

Use main beam when needed for a sufficient field of view, but not where the road is adequately lit, where it can dazzle an approaching driver or an adjacent rail/ship operator, or at close distance behind another vehicle. Dipped beam is the usual driving light. In fog or heavy precipitation, front fog lights may replace dipped beam; the prohibited combinations must not be used together. A rear fog light is restricted to fog, heavy precipitation or comparable reduced visibility and must not dazzle a following driver.

Make lighting and speed one decision. If you dip the lights and can see less far, reassess speed immediately. Check the edges of the visible road for people and animals rather than assuming a dark area is empty. Keep windows and mirrors clear enough for a useful view and learn demisting controls before a difficult journey.

Automatic lighting is an aid, not confirmation that every required lamp is on. In a car whose daytime-light mode leaves the rear lights off, check the actual setting when darkness or bad weather arrives.
Light and visual information

children.text: Lighting choice · Name the prohibited pair.

text.text: Do not use dipped headlights and front fog lights together. In fog or heavy precipitation, front fog lights may replace dipped headlights; they are not an extra light to add to them. Select a permitted mode and check it on the actual vehicle.

label.text: Transportstyrelsen: dipped beam and front fog lights

text.text: Central vision supplies the fine detail where you are looking directly. Reading the precise wording on a road sign relies particularly on it. Merely noticing a sign at the edge of your view does not establish what its text says.

Peripheral or side vision surrounds your direct focus. It can alert you to movement, a developing hazard or a traffic change outside that focus. Move your eyes, and head where needed, to inspect the relevant object directly while maintaining control and awareness of the road. For example, notice movement near the verge, then look to identify whether it is a person about to enter your path. Keep scanning; staring at one sign can leave other information unattended.

One approaching light at night does not prove a narrow motorcycle. A wider car can have a failed headlight. Transportstyrelsen documents defective car headlights; the practical inference is to allow for a vehicle whose full width is not yet visible. Preserve a safe lateral margin and adapt speed to the view rather than squeezing past on a guessed width.
Reassess the visible road

caption.text: Rain and darkness shorten the usable view. The teal car travels on the right. Reassess speed and check the actual exterior-light setting; the illustration does not identify a lamp mode or a measured stopping distance.

text.text: Rain becomes heavy during a daytime trip. The dashboard remains illuminated, but the driver checks and selects the appropriate exterior lighting rather than inferring that the rear lights must be on. The driver also reduces speed for the shorter usable view.
Check your understanding

(1) Can you maintain speed solely because the limit is unchanged after dipping main beam? (2) May dipped headlights and front fog lights be used together? (3) Which vision role reads precise sign text, and which can alert you to movement outside direct focus? (4) Does one approaching light prove a narrow motorcycle?
Adjust speed to the information the light actually gives you.

objectives.text: Choose a visibility and lighting strategy for darkness, fog and glare.

documents.title: Drive within what you can see

text.text: (1) No; adapt speed and gap. (2) Cold air cools it above and below. (3) A nearly invisible slippery ice layer. (4) Water mixes with accumulated dirt/oily residues. (5) To reduce rear grip loss, tail swing and rotation. (6) Oversteer: rear grip loss, tail outward, more rotation than intended. Understeer: front grip loss, less turn and a wider/straighter path. (7) A water film reduces effective tyre-road contact. Ease off the accelerator, keep steering steady and avoid abrupt steering/hard braking; use gentle necessary corrections.
Explain how surface conditions, tyres and driver inputs affect stability, steering and braking.

Tyres need friction to change the vehicle's speed and direction. Braking while cornering shares that capacity; ABS can help preserve steering forces during braking, but the available friction still limits the result. Water, snow and ice change the conditions at the tyre contact, so dry-road expectations cannot simply be carried into them.
Warnings about grip Independent slippery-road and loose-chippings warnings. Observe the actual surface; these warnings are not limited to winter.
Continue the learning

children.text: Requirements for ordinary light cars and their trailers, checked 1 October 2026.

text.text: Between 1 December and 31 March, winter tyres or equivalent equipment are required when winter conditions exist. Snow, ice, slush or frost on any part of the road counts; police determine conditions at the location. The minimum tread depth for the ordinary light-vehicle case is 3 mm. Studless winter tyres for the car need the mountain/snowflake marking.

Studded tyres are permitted from 1 October to 15 April and outside that period when winter conditions exist or are expected. Do not mix studded and non-studded tyres on an ordinary passenger car or light goods vehicle. In winter conditions, a studded towing car requires a studded trailer; the reverse combination is allowed. A light-trailer transition permits specified winter-designed M+S tyres through 30 November 2028. Exemptions and heavier-vehicle cases need their own checks; they are not the ordinary car rule.
Check local studded-tyre restrictions Seasonal permission to use studs does not override a local prohibition. This road sign is not a tyre sidewall marking.

For summer conditions, the minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm. Transportstyrelsen recommends placing the tyres with the best grip or greatest tread depth at the rear and checking pressure against the vehicle's instructions. A legal minimum is not a promise of equal performance in every condition.
Read changing surfaces

children.text: Surface change · A bridge can freeze first.

text.text: A bridge is exposed to cold air above and below. That exposure can cool it faster than neighbouring road supported by ground, so moisture can freeze on the bridge while the approach still appears clear. It is a possibility, not a rule that every bridge always freezes first. Anticipate uncertain grip and reduce speed before reaching the bridge.

children.text: Rain on a cold road · Ice can hide.

text.text: Rainwater can freeze when it meets a road surface cold enough for ice to form, producing a thin, nearly invisible slippery layer. The road may look wet, and the air temperature can be above zero while the surface is still below freezing. Near-zero air alone does not prove ice, but it calls for attention to surface conditions, more space and lower speed.

label.text: Trafikverket: deceptive ice and cold roads

children.text: First rain after dry weather · Residues matter.

text.text: During a dry spell, dust, dirt and oily residues can accumulate. The first rain can mix with these contaminants and make the road unusually slippery. Reassess speed and separation as rain starts; do not assume a light shower immediately washes the surface clean or that a fixed time restores grip.

label.text: County Fire: rain after a dry spell

text.text: A light shower begins after dry weather as you approach a bridge in near-freezing conditions. Plan for both wet residues and possible local ice. The clear-looking approach does not measure the grip on the bridge.
Understand grip and handling

children.text: Rear stability · Why the best grip belongs at the rear.

text.text: Transportstyrelsen recommends the best-grip or deepest-tread tyres at the rear to reduce skid risk in braking and bends, for both front- and rear-wheel-drive cars. Better rear grip helps reduce the risk of the rear sliding outward and rotating the car. Suitable tyres and stability assistance still cannot guarantee control.

label.text: Transportstyrelsen: best tyres at the rear

text.text: In the loss-of-grip situation, the rear tyres lose sufficient lateral grip, the tail swings outward and the car rotates more than intended into the turn. This can develop into a spin.

In the loss-of-grip situation, the front tyres cannot supply the lateral grip needed for the requested turn. The car turns less than intended and follows a straighter, wider path; adding more steering does not guarantee the requested curve. These are grip-loss explanations, not a full definition of every vehicle's normal handling characteristics.

If water builds between tyres and road, it can support the tyre on a film and reduce or remove effective tyre-road contact. Steering and braking then have less grip to work with. Reduce speed before standing water and uncertain wet surfaces.

If aquaplaning starts and there is space to slow gradually, ease off the accelerator, keep steering steady and avoid abrupt steering or hard braking. Make only gentle necessary corrections as contact returns. This is different from

's ABS emergency-stop instruction: ABS cannot create grip where a tyre is separated from the road by water. An immediate collision emergency needs action appropriate to the actual situation; this advice does not establish a universal ban on braking.

A rear slide swinging the tail outward is oversteer; a front slide that prevents the intended curve is understeer. A light, unresponsive steering feel over standing water raises a different possibility: aquaplaning. Recognise the mechanism, preserve margins and practise vehicle-specific emergency handling only with suitable instruction.
Prepare before grip changes

Reduce speed and increase space before reaching uncertain grip. Avoid demanding abrupt braking, steering and acceleration together. Do not experiment with skid recovery in ordinary traffic. Establish the actual vehicle's emergency-braking behaviour through appropriate instruction and risk training.

caption.text: A dry-looking foreground leads towards a shaded winter bend. The surface appearance is a reason to reassess, not a measurement of friction. No skid-recovery technique or guaranteed tyre performance is shown.

text.text: Your car has suitable winter tyres, but the next bend is partly shaded and looks different from the road behind. You reduce speed before the bend and preserve margin. Equipment does not establish the grip at that particular point.
Check your understanding

(1) Does legal tread depth guarantee dry-road spacing on ice? (2) Why can a bridge freeze first? (3) What can rain form on a sufficiently cold road? (4) Why can first rain after dry weather be unusually slippery? (5) Why place the best-grip tyres at the rear? (6) Compare oversteer and understeer in a grip-loss situation. (7) What is aquaplaning, and how should you respond when there is room to slow gradually?
Tyres and assistance systems support a cautious plan; they do not create unlimited grip.

objectives.text: Explain how surface conditions, tyres and driver inputs affect stability, steering and braking.

text.text: No. Equipment use must not adversely affect driving. Prepare it while parked or stop somewhere safe and lawful.
Recognise distraction, stress and fatigue and choose an interruption or alternative travel plan.

During road travel, a driver may use communication equipment only if it does not adversely affect driving. Holding the equipment in the hand while using it is prohibited. Hands-free use is therefore not automatically acceptable: the effect on driving still matters. You must also not drive when exhaustion or another condition prevents safe control.

Prepare navigation before setting off, place the phone away from casual handling and agree when passengers can help. If a conversation, screen task or emotional reaction is consuming the attention needed for the road, end it. A safe place to stop is the place to resolve a complicated route or urgent message.
Use
's notice-then-inspect distinction when scanning. A conversation that consumes attention can delay recognising what peripheral vision has alerted you to.

Treat fatigue as a reason to change the journey. Plan rest opportunities and stop safely when concentration cannot be maintained. Do not wait for a dramatic event to prove that you are too tired. Trafikverket recommends setting out rested, allowing time and taking breaks on longer journeys. No universal break interval in this material certifies that you can continue safely.
Plan a safe rest stop A rest-area destination can support journey planning. The sign gives no prescribed break interval or assurance that a tired driver can safely continue.
Protect attention before moving

caption.text: A left-hand-seat driver is parked in a parking area, with the phone in a holder. This is a stopped discussion, not permission to use a screen or conduct a distracting call while driving. Controls and mounting are illustrative.

text.text: A driver misses a sign during an intense hands-free conversation. The useful response is not to argue that the device is legal to use. End the conversation, reassess fitness and stop safely if attention cannot be restored.
Check your understanding
Is entering a destination on a mounted phone necessarily allowed because it is not hand-held?
Protect attention before it is fully occupied.

objectives.text: Recognise distraction, stress and fatigue and choose an interruption or alternative travel plan.

text.text: It may show that reassessment worked. The aim is a safe decision under current conditions, not loyalty to an earlier plan.
Reassess a trip when weather, darkness, delays or passenger pressure accumulate.

At a meaningful change—worsening visibility, an unexpected closure, a missed rest opportunity—review the whole plan. Ask what has changed in the driver, vehicle, route and time available. A manageable single difficulty may become demanding when several occur together. This is a planning exercise, not a formula that assigns a numerical risk score.

Choose between continuing with a suitable margin, stopping safely, changing route, changing driver if lawful and suitable, or cancelling the journey. The choice depends on the actual conditions. A driver unable to maintain safe control must not continue merely because the destination is close.

The syllabus treats route choice, timing, passengers, fatigue and personal motives as parts of driving competence. Use the same questions after a journey: Which warning did I notice early? Which did I explain away because I wanted to finish?
Reconsider the whole journey

caption.text: Two adults reconsider a journey indoors while rain falls outside and the car remains parked. Use the available route information to choose a realistic alternative before setting off.

text.text: A late appointment leaves a driver facing an unfamiliar route in darkness and worsening weather. Instead of protecting the original arrival time, the driver finds a safe stopping place, tells the person waiting and chooses a realistic alternative. The change happens while there is still time to make it calmly.
Check your understanding
Is deciding to cancel evidence that the original plan failed?
Replanning is a driving skill.

text.text: (1) No. The at-most-750 kg trailer route can cover it; technical/actual-weight limits still apply. (2) The road maximum, with speed reduced for conditions. It is not the general heavy-lorry cap or a target; towing needs a separate combination check.
Use entitlement and vehicle information to assess a car or trailer combination.

Ordinary category B permits a passenger car or light goods vehicle with a total weight of no more than 3,500 kg. For trailers, either the trailer's total weight is at most 750 kg, or, if above 750 kg, the car and trailer's combined total weights must not exceed 3,500 kg. The first route can therefore permit a combination up to 4,250 kg; it does not mean every 4,250 kg combination is permitted on ordinary B.

Extended B (B96) permits combined total weights up to 4,250 kg, without increasing the car's 3,500 kg limit. Under the ordinary current BE rule, the towing car is still limited to 3,500 kg total weight and the trailer or trailers may have combined total weights up to 3,500 kg. Older entitlements and conditions can differ; check the individual licence rather than applying a current-new-licence example to everyone. This book is not a full B96 or BE course.

Entitlement uses registered total weights. Technical towing limits also restrict what the particular car may pull in its actual loaded state. Emptying a trailer may reduce its actual weight without changing its registered total weight, so it may solve a technical-weight problem but not an entitlement problem.

children.text: Vehicle comparison · Light lorry without a trailer.

text.text: A light lorry (

) has a registered total weight of at most 3,500 kg. Without a trailer, it normally follows the road's maximum speed; the general heavy-lorry cap does not apply. A heavy lorry exceeds 3,500 kg: without a trailer its vehicle maximum is 90 km/h on a motorway or expressway, and 80 km/h on other roads; with a trailer it is 80 km/h. A lower road limit always applies. For a light lorry towing, check the combination rules in

A light lorry without a trailer on a road signed 100 km/h does not acquire an 80 km/h cap simply because it is called a lorry. Still reduce speed for visibility, grip, traffic and load; a maximum is not a target.
Two separate checks

caption.text: Hypothetical registered total weights: 2,200 kg + 1,500 kg = 3,700 kg. Check entitlement and technical limits separately. The pictured vehicle does not establish its capacity.

text.text: A car has a total weight of 2,200 kg and a trailer 1,500 kg. Their combined total weight is 3,700 kg, and the trailer exceeds 750 kg. Ordinary B does not cover this combination. B96 may satisfy the entitlement part, but the car's towing capacity and loaded weights still need checking.
Check your understanding
(1) Is ordinary B automatically excluded for a 3,500 kg car and 750 kg trailer? (2) Which maximum normally applies to a light lorry without a trailer, and is it a target?

Keep within the car's permitted trailer weight and maximum actual combined weight as well as each vehicle's limits. Registration fields O.1/O.2 identify relevant braked/unbraked trailer limits; F.3 identifies the maximum combined actual weight. Missing or unclear data needs resolution before towing.

Secure cargo so it cannot endanger people, fall, drag, obstruct control or obscure required lights and signals. Put heavy items low and suitably supported, and follow the equipment's rated load and securing instructions. A roof box is not permission to exceed a roof or vehicle limit.

Projecting cargo needs separate checks. Mark cargo extending ahead or more than 1 m behind, with the specified exception for clearly visible front projection below 1 m. Darkness or poor visibility requires the prescribed lamps and reflectors, white forward and red rearward. Marking does not authorise an otherwise prohibited width, length or load.

On roads other than private roads, the ordinary width/load rule restricts a motor vehicle or its trailer if the load projects more than 20 cm beyond either side, or the overall width including load exceeds 260 cm. The general length ceiling for a non-bus vehicle or combination is 24.0 m including load; special regimes and exemptions exist. Do not treat those general ceilings as permission to exceed a lower vehicle, route or sign limit. Special oversized transport needs its own verification.

Dimensions and bearing capacity Independent examples distinguish width, height, length, a width plate and bearing-capacity classes. A general vehicle limit does not override a lower signed restriction.

For a conventional light braked trailer with rigid drawbar and suitable overrun brake, the maximum is normally 80 km/h. For an unbraked trailer up to 750 kg, 80 km/h requires its total weight to be no more than half the car’s defined ready weight; when the trailer is empty, its ready weight is used for this comparison instead. The ordinary unbraked combination outside those conditions is limited to 40 km/h, subject to the other combination requirements; other configurations can be limited to 30. Use Transportstyrelsen's calculator and guidance for the specific combination, and obey any lower road limit.

Check coupling load
Towball load (

) is the trailer's downward load at the coupling, not the trailer's whole loaded weight. With a conventional towball behind the car's rear axle, excessive downward force acts through a lever arm: it increases rear loading while reducing the load carried by the front axle. Front unloading does not require the wheels to leave the road. With less front-tyre loading, available steering grip and response can be impaired.

label.text: Official towing guide: front-wheel unloading, page 6

text.text: Trafikverket warns that incorrect coupling pressure can lift the car or trailer. Follow the specified towball, coupling, axle and vehicle limits for the actual combination; there is no universal number in this lesson. Measure and redistribute the load as instructed before travelling. Total trailer weight, coupling load and cargo securing are separate checks. Do not cure excessive downward load by guessing or creating an equally unsuitable load distribution.

label.text: Official towing guide: ratings and load distribution

text.text: Your total trailer weight is within the car's towing limit, but a heavy object far forward makes the coupling load excessive. The total-weight check has not proved suitable axle loading. Stop preparation, establish the specified limits and adjust and secure the load before driving.
Know the actual load

caption.text: Hypothetical loading calculation: 400 kg ready weight + 500 kg cargo = 900 kg actual weight. Example towing limit: 800 kg. The goods are beside the trailer for planning; this is not a secured-load demonstration.

text.text: A trailer's ready weight is 400 kg and cargo adds 500 kg, giving an illustrative actual weight of 900 kg. A car rated to tow only 800 kg cannot pull that load merely because the driver's entitlement covers the registered total weights.
Check your understanding
(1) Does a strap prove the vehicle is within its weight limit? (2) Can an acceptable total trailer weight still conceal excessive towball load, and what can that do?
Establish what the load weighs, where it is, how it is restrained and what limits apply.
